doc.title: Etta Jones interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 2, 1998

title: The hit "Don't Go To Strangers" and its effects
summary: The song won a gold record after ten years of rejection; her pay jumped from $50 to $750 a weekend, and she gained friends across the country.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Studio work and jingles: New York session life

blocks.x: You’re welcome. “Don’t Go To Strangers” it was a really nice hit for you. At that time, what did people consider a hit? How many records?

Well I got a gold record for that one so I don’t know exactly in terms of numbers. But I was always under the impression that when you sold a million copies or close to it, you got a gold record. I don’t know if that’s true or not, but I do have a gold record for “Don’t Go To Strangers.” And I tried to do that song for ten years. But it wasn’t commercial they said. Each time I would want to put it on an album. “That’s not commercial.” You know because they always think they know what might go and what might not go. But you never know. And you will never know. Something — it just went. I guess the people were ready for something that they could relate to. “Don’t Go To Strangers” people started saying it. It was just, I’m glad I didn’t do it ten years ahead of time because maybe it wouldn’t have been—

Right. And so all of a sudden I went from $50 a weekend to $750 a weekend. It was frightening. I just couldn’t stand it. I couldn’t stand all the attention. How would you like your hair? How would you like to do— It was bugging me. I’m not a person that likes a lot of fanfare.
Yeah, for people to wait on you.

No. They said well let me help you — I said wait a minute I can put on my own shoes. No thank you. So I think now if I had a big hit again I could deal with it. I would know how to handle it. But then it was very trying.
And you were how old then?
I think — was I 28? Something like that.

It was ‘59. And it developed in ‘60 really, when they started playing it. It was coming out of the stores, it was on the juke box. And a friend of mine came and he said, “Your record is on the—” I said get out of here, don’t tell me that. He said, “Yep, come on, let’s go, I’ll let you see.” And when you get on the juke box and they’re playing it and you hear it coming from record stores—you know that you’ve got something going.
Yeah, and you weren’t even aware that it was happening.

I wasn’t aware. But I heard Symphony Sid play it and Mort Feeger, on the radio. And I thought wait, I thought maybe it was going to be played once or twice, you know, but they started playing it and they started, I couldn’t believe it. I was so grateful, because it meant travel, it meant better clubs, it meant more money. But the money wasn’t really that important to me, I mean I just loved to sing so much, and I wanted to get paid, I mean it’s not unimportant, I wanted to get paid a decent salary and I wanted to work in a decent place. And so the record afforded me that, it really gave me — and one thing about going on the road and having something that would make people know you, you get to have a lot of friends. I have friends across the country. I have so many keys to so many —

People’s houses. When I said that one time I said oh wait a minute now, I have keys to families, not keys to different guys. But it made me have so many friends and I’ll never forget this singing business for that. I have so many across the country. And they wait ‘till I come. “She’s coming next week,” or, “she’ll be here.” They start calling each other you know. And I have friends that never see each other until I come.
So it’s really nice. I love my job. I really do.
